parent.name: King's Gambit Declined: Queen's Knight Defense
Nimzo-Larsen Attack
parent.overview: 1.b3 prepares Bb2 on the long diagonal, a hypermodern way to control the centre and pressure Black's kingside from the flank. Black's two main replies are 1...e5 (2.Bb2 Nc6 3.e3, the most common) and 1...d5 (2.Bb2 Nf6 3.e3, often a reversed Nimzo-Indian). White's usual set-up is e3, Nf3, Bb2 with flexible pawn play (f4, c4, d3, a kingside fianchetto), choosing a central plan after seeing Black's set-up. Black may take a big d5/e5 centre for White to undermine, contest d5 with ...c5/c4 English-style, or play London-like set-ups. Theory is light, most lines are rated roughly equal, and the play can turn tactical once the long diagonal and central files open. It is used as a surprise weapon by super-GMs, especially in online blitz.

parent.name: Italian Game: Giuoco Piano
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Bc5
parent.overview: Both sides develop the king's bishop to its active diagonal (Bc4 and ...Bc5), eyeing f7/f2. White's choice at move 4 decides the character. Slow lines are 4.c3 followed by d3 or d4 and the modern Giuoco Pianissimo with d3 (Re1, Nbd2-f1-g3, a4, h3): White postpones any central clash and the game is a patient manoeuvring battle. The sharper lines are the classical 4.c3 Nf6 5.d4 (Greco's Attack, Moller Attack), where White sacrifices a pawn for initiative, and the Evans Gambit 4.b4, a pawn for rapid development and an attack on f7. The Three Knights 4.Nc3 and 4.O-O are also main subtree moves. Black mirrors development, challenges the centre with ...d5, and has sufficient defensive resources. It is a respected choice used by Karpov and, as a Ruy Lopez sidestep, by Carlsen.

parent.name: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation
parent.overview: This root is the King's Indian reached by the move order 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.c4 (the same position as 3.Nf3 in the 2.c4 move order). It is not a distinct opening: it is the ordinary King's Indian, where Black fianchettoes with ...Bg7, castles, and strikes at White's centre with ...e5, ...c5 or ...f5. White's choice of set-up decides the character: the classical 4.Nc3 and e4 leads to the locked-centre opposite-wing race (c4-c5 against ...f5-f4), while the Fianchetto Variation (g3, Bg2, O-O, Nc3) is quieter, positional, and has less forcing theory. The data subtree groups 4.e4 Normal Variation lines (the majority of games) under this root, so it mixes both. Black's success depends on timing and coordination rather than automatic aggression.

parent.name: Owen Defense
parent.overview: Black plays 1...b6 to fianchetto the queen's bishop on b7 and attack e4 from a distance, letting White take the centre with 2.d4 and then undermining it with ...e6, ...Nf6, ...Bb4 and the breaks ...c5 or ...d5. The main line is 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bd3 e6 4.Nf3 c5 5.c3, with 3.Nc3 (French-like) and 3.Nf3 also played. Black's kingside is a little loose and White is described as getting a space advantage and, with sensible play, a slight edge (Bauer) or around 60% wins in practice. Theory calls it slightly unsound but not refuted; it is rare at top level in classical play, although Carlsen, Nakamura and Firouzja have used it in online blitz. The 3...f5 Matovinsky Gambit is described as suicidal by Bauer.

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...c6 to support ...d5 and so challenges the e4 pawn with a sound pawn structure, while keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out to f5 or g4 before ...e6 (the French Defence's main drawback, at the cost of a tempo). Black accepts less space early and tends to get a resilient, hard-to-break structure with few weaknesses and good endgame prospects. Play is mostly positional and manoeuvring; it is called more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian (s1). The Advance (3.e5 Bf5) and Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4) lines are more combative, and the Advance became the most popular White try in the 21st century. Main branches: Classical (4...Bf5), Advance, Exchange, Panov, 4...Nf6 lines, Gurgenidze (...g6), Two Knights (2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3) and Fantasy (3.f3). This is a crossroads root after 1...c6; the pawn structures differ by branch.

parent.name: Philidor Defense: Exchange Variation
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 exd4
parent.overview: After 3.d4 exd4 White recaptures (4.Nxd4 is the main line; Morphy's 4.Qxd4 is the alternative) and then has a space advantage and the more comfortable game. Black replies ...Nf6 and ...Be7, castles quickly and aims for a compact position (often with ...Nbd7 or ...c5/...c6 later) with king safety first, using ...d5 or ...c5 as freeing breaks. The structure is passive but not refuted: White cannot force a tactical win, but must prove an edge. Sources call it a sound, practical defence, an easy entry point for club players that is rarely used by top players because it concedes space; Aronian is mentioned as an occasional user. The Antoshin set-up (6.Be2) is a common White try.
